newsitem.title: USA: CFTC appeals panel ruling on Frankwell Bullion case.
newsitem.headline: CFTC appeals panel ruling on Frankwell Bullion case.

text.p: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission said Friday it filed a petition requesting a full federal appeals court rehearing of a decision dismissing the agency's lawsuit against Frankwell Bullion Ltd. for lack of jurisdiction.

The petition was directed to the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, a panel of which issued the ruling on Oct. 29. The ruling affirmed a 1995 lower court decision limiting the CFTC's jurisdiction over foreign currency transactions.

Frankwell Bullion, a Hong Kong-based brokerage with operations in the United States, had been charged by the CFTC, which regulates U.S. futures markets, with violation of the U.S. Commodity Exchange Act in connection with the firm's sales of off-exchange foreign currency futures contracts.

The case was been closely watched because the CFTC's stance on its jurisdiction conflicted with those of the Treasury and the Securities and Exchange Commission as well as with big banks and brokerage houses.
The case centres on the scope of the so-called Treasury Amendment, passed by Congress in 1974 at the behest of the Treasury Department to limit the CFTC's jurisdiction.
The appeals court panel decision rejected the CFTC's contention that its jurisdiction extended to any association selling foreign currency futures.

In its petition, the CFTC argued that the panel's decision stripped the agency of power to protect the general public from fraud and abuse in the sale of off-exchange foreign currency futures contracts.

It also contended that the decision ignored the intent of Congress that transactions by the public in foreign currency futures be given the same regulatory protections given to customers in other fugures marketrs.

Furthermore, the CFTC said, the decision for the first time creates a "regulatory gap" in which no federal agency is empowered to protect the public from fraud arising from fraud arising from the sale of foreign currency futures contracts.
Daniel Waldman, CFTC general counsel, said "fraud in the offer and sale of off-exchange futures contracts on foreign currencies is a growing problem in this country."
"We view the panel's decision as a setback in our fight to protect the public from unscrupulous bucket shop and boiler room operators selling foreign currency futures to the public."
The CFTC said it expects action on its petition this winter.

The U.S. Supreme Court is separately considering a similar case, CFTC v. Dunn, which is tied to the interpretation of the scope of the Treasury Amendment. The CFTC said a decision on the case is expected by the spring of 1997.
